questions.questionText:
Mapwork Skills:
(a) Describe how to calculate the gradient between two points A (altitude 1,420 m) and B (altitude 1,220 m) located 4.0 cm apart on a 1:50 000 map. [4 marks]
(b) State two clues on a 1:50 000 map showing that an area practises commercial irrigated agriculture. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Vertical rise = 1,420 - 1,220 = 200 m [1]. Horizontal distance = 4.0 cm × 50,000 = 200,000 cm = 2,000 m [1]. Gradient = 200 / 2,000 = 1 in 10 [2].
(b) Presence of dams/weirs, canals/furrows, green orchard/plantation symbols, regular dip tanks/farm roads [2].

questions.questionText:
With reference to a named tropical savanna area in Zimbabwe (e.g., Hwange or Gonarezhou):
(a) Describe three physical characteristics of savanna vegetation and climate. [3 marks]
(b) Explain two ways wildlife/trees adapt to the long dry winter season. [4 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Distinct hot wet summer (Nov–Mar) and cool dry winter (May–Aug); scattered drought-resistant trees (baobab, mopane, acacia) amid tall seasonal savanna grasses [3].
(b) Trees shed leaves in dry season, grow thick fire-resistant bark, or store water in swollen trunks (baobab); wildlife migrate along rivers/pans [4].

questions.questionText: Explain the formation of an ox-bow lake along the mature/lower course of a meandering river like the Lower Zambezi or Limpopo. [6 marks]
questions.explanation:
1. River erodes faster on outer concave bends (helicoidal flow) and deposits silt on inner convex slip-off slopes, exaggerating meander loops [2].
2. Neck between two bends narrows continuously [1].
3. During a flood, high-energy water cuts straight across the narrow neck [2].
4. Deposition seals off the old loop, leaving a crescent-shaped ox-bow lake cut off from the main channel [1].

questions.questionText: Compare relief (orographic) rainfall in Zimbabwe's Eastern Highlands (Chimanimani/Nyanga) with convectional rainfall on the Highveld. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Relief rainfall: Moist SE trade winds from Indian Ocean rise over Chimanimani mountains, cool adiabatically, condense, and drop heavy rain on windward slopes leaving a dry rain shadow (Save Valley) to the west [3]. Convectional rainfall: Intense afternoon ground heating warms moist air, creating rising thermals, tall cumulonimbus clouds, heavy short afternoon thunderstorms and lightning [3].

questions.questionText:
With reference to gold or platinum mining in Zimbabwe:
(a) State three economic benefits of mining to the country. [3 marks]
(b) Describe three negative environmental impacts of unregulated alluvial/artisanal gold panning and suggest two solutions. [5 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Earns foreign currency, creates direct/indirect jobs, builds roads/clinics/power infrastructure, and generates tax royalties [3].
(b) River siltation, mercury/cyanide poisoning of streams, dangerous uncovered pits, and deforestation [3]. Solutions: Formalise/licence syndicates under EMA supervision, ban river-bed digging, and enforce pit backfilling & mercury-free retorts [2].

questions.questionText:
(a) Distinguish between internal migration and international migration, giving one Zimbabwean example of each. [4 marks]
(b) Outline four problems caused by rapid rural-to-urban migration in Harare or Bulawayo. [4 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Internal: moving within borders (e.g., rural villages to Harare for work). International: crossing national borders (e.g., emigrating to South Africa or UK) [4].
(b) Overcrowded informal housing/slums, burst sewage & clean-water shortages, traffic congestion, rising urban unemployment & strain on clinics/schools [4].

questions.questionText: Explain four strategies Zimbabwe is using to reduce power load-shedding and diversify away from over-reliance on Kariba hydroelectricity during droughts. [4 marks]
questions.explanation: 1. Expanding Hwange Thermal Power Station (Units 7 & 8). 2. Developing utility solar farms (e.g., Gwanda/Nyabira) and rooftop net-metering solar. 3. Importing electricity via the Southern African Power Pool (SAPP). 4. Promoting biogas and solar water geysers to cut peak grid load [4 marks].

questions.questionText: Describe three human causes of desertification/land degradation in Zimbabwe's communal areas and explain three sustainable reclamation methods. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Causes: Overgrazing above carrying capacity, cutting trees for firewood/tobacco curing, and ploughing down steep slopes/stream banks [3]. Reclamation: Community woodlots & solar stoves, rotational grazing paddocks, gully gabions/vetiver grass, and Pfumvudza conservation farming [3].

questions.questionText: Outline the inputs, processes, and outputs of commercial sugarcane production at Triangle/Hippo Valley in the SE Lowveld, explaining why irrigation is vital there. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Inputs: Flat alluvial soils, Lake Mutirikwi/Tugwi-Mukosi irrigation water, sugarcane setts, fertilisers, tractors, labour [2]. Processes: Land preparation, canal/drip irrigation, weeding, cane burning & harvesting, crushing at sugar mills [2]. Outputs: Raw/refined brown sugar, molasses, ethanol (Chisumbanje/Triangle), bagasse power [1]. Irrigation is essential because Lowveld rainfall (<450 mm) is far too low for cane [1].

questions.questionText: State three advantages and three disadvantages of multinational manufacturing industries operating in Zimbabwean cities. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Advantages: Bring foreign capital & modern technology, create skilled jobs & local supplier contracts, pay corporate taxes [3]. Disadvantages: Profits often repatriated abroad, can out-compete small local firms, risk industrial air/effluent pollution if unregulated [3].

questions.questionText: Explain the Greenhouse Effect vs Enhanced Global Warming, and state two observable impacts of climate change on Zimbabwean agriculture. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Natural greenhouse gases (CO₂, H₂O vapour, CH₄) trap outgoing infrared heat keeping Earth habitable (~15°C); human fossil-fuel burning & deforestation increase these gases causing excess warming [3]. Zimbabwe impacts: Later erratic rainfall onset, more frequent mid-season dry spells, and intense cyclones like Cyclone Idai damaging crops and dams [2].

questions.questionText: Describe four factors influencing the location of a heavy iron & steel works (such as ZISCO/Manhize). [4 marks]
questions.explanation: 1. Proximity to bulky raw materials (iron ore, limestone, coking coal) to slash transport costs. 2. Reliable bulk water supply for cooling. 3. Heavy rail/road transport links. 4. Flat cheap industrial land near reliable high-voltage power [4 marks].

questions.questionText: Contrast rural settlement patterns (dispersed, nucleated, linear) and state two geographic factors favouring a nucleated rural village. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Dispersed: isolated homesteads spread across large farms. Nucleated: houses clustered tightly around a central point. Linear: dwellings aligned along a road, river, or ridge [3]. Nucleated factors: shared borehole/water source, defensive hillside, or fertile pocket of valley soil [2].

questions.questionText: Explain what a GIS (Geographic Information System) is and give three practical ways Zimbabwean planners use GIS & Remote Sensing. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: GIS captures, stores, analyses, and displays layered spatial/map data tied to geographic coordinates [2]. Uses: Monitoring deforestation & veld fires via satellite imagery; mapping urban water/sewer burst pipes; tracking wildlife poaching/drought crop yields [3].

questions.questionText: Draw/describe a simple sketch of a volcano at a destructive plate boundary and list two benefits and two hazards of living near volcanic regions. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Oceanic plate subducts beneath continental plate, melting into magma that rises through cracks to build steep composite volcanoes [2]. Benefits: Mineral-rich fertile volcanic soils, geothermal power, and tourism [2]. Hazards: Pyroclastic flows, lahars/mudflows, toxic ash suffocating crops and roofs [2].

questions.questionText: Describe the Demographic Transition Model's (DTM) Stage 2 and Stage 4, stating why Zimbabwe has shifted from high death rates toward slower population growth. [5 marks]
questions.explanation: Stage 2: High birth rate + rapidly falling death rate -> rapid natural population increase (improved sanitation, clinics, vaccines) [2]. Stage 4: Low birth rate + low death rate -> slow/stable growth [2]. Better clean water, immunisation, girls' secondary education, and family planning reduced infant mortality and fertility [1].

questions.questionText: Explain how the CAMPFIRE programme in Zimbabwe links wildlife conservation with rural community development. [4 marks]
questions.explanation: CAMPFIRE grants rural district councils/villages rights to manage local wildlife sustainably and earn revenue from photographic safaris and controlled quotas [2]. Revenue builds local schools, clinics, and boreholes, turning villagers into stakeholders who deter poaching instead of seeing wildlife only as crop pests [2].

questions.questionText: Compare road transport and air transport for Zimbabwe's horticultural exports (flowers/fresh peas to Europe), justifying the best choice. [4 marks]
questions.explanation: Air transport moves perishable fresh flowers/vegetables from Harare to Europe within hours, preserving freshness despite high freight cost per kg [2]. Road/sea freight takes weeks and spoils fresh produce, though suited to non-perishable citrus/tobacco [2]. Air wins for high-value perishables.

questions.questionText:
A student carries out fieldwork measuring downstream changes in river velocity and pebble size along a local stream.
(a) State how the student safely measures stream surface velocity. [3 marks]
(b) State the expected trend in pebble size from source to mouth and explain why. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
(a) Measure a straight 10 m bank section; drop an orange/cork float at the upstream line, time how long it takes to reach 10 m, repeat 3 times for average velocity = 10 m / mean time [3].
(b) Pebbles become smaller and smoother/rounder downstream due to attrition (colliding rocks chipping corners off) and abrasion [2].

questions.questionText: Identify three major causes of urban traffic congestion in Zimbabwean cities and suggest three sustainable urban transport solutions. [6 marks]
questions.explanation: Causes: High commuter growth into single CBD, unscheduled kombis stopping on carriageways, broken traffic signals/potholes [3]. Solutions: Dedicated bus rapid transit (BRT)/urban rail lanes, park-and-ride hubs, synchronised solar traffic lights & ring-road bypasses [3].
